summary: New page published: AI skills assessment validation: 6 studies from our report
added_text:
In short
This article summarizes Codility’s AI for Business technical report, version 2.0, which sets out 6 studies on the validity, reliability and fairness of its AI skills assessment for business roles. The
full report
, with every method, table and limitation, is free to download. In live hiring, scores rose with an expert’s ratings at every level. No meaningful gender differences were found. The evidence supports using scores from 2 or more tasks to rank candidates for a shortlist, with a person reviewing mid-range scores.
Candidates use an AI Assistant to work through a realistic business problem and hand in a short written deliverable. Fixed rules score it against a rubric written for each task, so the same answer always gets the same score, and no generative AI model is involved.
In live hiring, a trained expert rated 96 applicants from 1 to 5. The engine’s average score rose with every step up that scale, from 37% for applicants rated 1 to 87% for those rated 5.
A first-pass check of all 53 longer tasks, the ones that take 20 to 50 minutes, found defects in 28. Tasks that an external AI tool such as ChatGPT could answer from the description alone are scheduled for redesign and retesting.
Decisions should rest on at least 2 tasks, and 3 or more when the stakes are high.
No meaningful score differences were found between women and men. Racial and ethnic differences were small on average, and at selective passing scores some groups fell below four-fifths of the highest group’s pass rate, so each employer should set its own passing score and monitor pass rates.
No score built from a candidate’s conversation with the AI is used in hiring decisions.
Evidence that scores predict job performance has not yet been established.
Since May, our team has talked with talent leaders, people-analytics teams and industrial-organizational psychologists at customer organizations about assessing AI skills. The request we hear most often is to see a candidate use AI on a realistic task. The psychologists and legal reviewers then go further. They want to know exactly how the score is produced, and they ask for evidence on whether it predicts performance and whether it disadvantages any group of candidates.
That is a reasonable thing to ask of any selection procedure, and a hard one to answer in a category this new. In October our team reviewed about 30 vendors selling assessments of AI skills. None of them published evidence on reliability, on whether scores predict job performance, or on adverse impact for an assessment in which a live AI takes part in the task.
Our answer is the
AI for Business technical report, version 2.0
, which covers 6 studies run between April and October 2026. This article summarizes it study by study. See who can design a system that scales
System design rounds are time-consuming, and they usually need a senior engineer in the room. Codility’s system design tasks show you before the interview: candidates build infrastructure on a board, send a rush of traffic through it and get a score automatically, with no code to write. The demo below is an interactive reproduction of those tasks: watch it play for a minute, then try a mission yourself.
What the demo shows
A reproduction of one mission for a fictional food delivery app, start to finish: a design that fails, the troubleshooting and a design that passes.
A brief from the business
Each mission sets the traffic to handle, the success rate to hit and a budget for the infrastructure.
Built on a board, with no code
Candidates add servers, load balancers, caches and databases from a catalog, then wire them up so requests flow from the internet to the database.
Test the design under traffic
The Test system button sends the mission’s traffic through the design, like a load test. Candidates can test as often as they like.
A failed test shows symptoms
It names each overloaded machine, with its load and its capacity. Finding the fix is up to the candidate.
Cost is part of the answer
Every machine has a price. A passing design under the cost target earns a bonus, so a lean design scores higher than an oversized one.
The same scoring for every candidate
The score counts the missions passed, plus the cost bonus. Every candidate is scored by the same rules, so you can compare results across a whole hiring round.
Two system design tasks in the Codility library
Both use the same board, and each asks a different question.
